title: U-A-Goose
text:
University of Alberta · Department of Computing Science
        U-A-Goose
        GrOup Of Software Engineering
        
          
          We study trustworthy software engineering in the AI era, asking: How can we help AI learn from limited, incomplete experience to reliably build and evolve complex software systems?
          We use software engineering knowledge to shape better learning objectives, experiences, and feedback, helping models explore beyond established solutions and refine their judgments in light of verifiable evidence.
        
        
          CourseWinter 2027
          CMPUT 663: AI for Software Engineering ↗
          We will offer this course in Winter 2027. For UofA students interested in doing research with us, we strongly recommend taking this course.

        Principal InvestigatorProf. Zhou YangAssistant ProfessorUniversity of AlbertaCanada CIFAR AI ChairAmii FellowHomepageEmailScholar
        Zhou Yang is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Computing Science at the University of Alberta, a Canada CIFAR AI Chair, and an Amii Fellow. He completed his Ph.D. at Singapore Management University in early 2025, after earning an MSc from University College London. He previously served as a senior research engineer at the Centre for Research on Intelligent Software Engineering.
His research establishes scientific and practical foundations for trustworthy code LLMs, integrating robustness, security, privacy, ecosystem understanding, and efficiency to support safer AI adoption in software engineering. He has received multiple major awards, including the 2026 MSR Outstanding Doctoral Research Award, the 2025 ACM SIGSOFT Outstanding Doctoral Dissertation Award, and the 2024 IEEE Computer Society Best Paper Award.

      Join the groupzy25@ualberta.ca ↗
      We welcome self-motivated students interested in software engineering, trustworthy AI, and code LLM research.
      
        Graduate studyPhD / Master by ResearchApplications for Fall 2027 are now open, but only very limited positions are available.Contact zy25@ualberta.ca with your CV, transcript, and a brief description of your research interests.
        Research experienceResearch assistantsFor current University of Alberta students, including ECE Master's students and undergraduates, interested in joining the group as research assistants.Send your CV and transcript to zy25@ualberta.ca.
        Individual studiesCMPUT 399 / CMPUT 499For University of Alberta undergraduates interested in taking an individual study course with the group.Contact zy25@ualberta.ca with your CV and transcript.
      
      
        Getting startedAll prospective research assistants and individual study students go through a lightweight screening process, which typically involves:
        01ReadA few selected papers relevant to your intended research area.02PresentA short talk to demonstrate your understanding of the papers.03ImplementReproduce or implement baseline methods.
        We consider academic merits, prior research experience, and alignment with the group's research directions to assess research potential and ensure a good mutual fit.

title: CMPUT 663: AI for Software Engineering
text:
← Back to U-A-Goose
  
    Winter 2027 · University of Alberta
    CMPUT 663: AI for Software Engineering
    
      TermWinter 2027
      InstructorProf. Zhou Yang
      DepartmentComputing Science
    
  

  
    Course overview
    This graduate course explores how AI is built and used for software engineering, with a focus on large language models of code and coding agents. It connects these systems to software engineering tasks and examines how to evaluate their usefulness, reliability, and limitations.
    The course brings together software engineering and machine learning, including the security, privacy, and human factors that matter when AI is used in real software development.
    Interested in research? For University of Alberta students interested in doing research with us, we strongly recommend taking this course.
  

  
    Course timeline
    15 teaching weeks · 2 classes per week · Reading Week excluded
    
      
        Week 01
        
          Introduction to Software Engineering
          This week introduces the goals, processes, tasks, and challenges of software engineering, covering requirements engineering, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance. Students will become familiar with software representations, formal specifications, testing, fuzzing, program analysis, agile development, and modern development tools, providing a foundation for understanding the engineering problems that AI can help address.
        
      
      
        Week 02
        
          Research Methods in Software Engineering
          This week introduces the research process in software engineering, including research questions and hypotheses, literature search and review, research design and evaluation, academic writing, and peer review. Students will learn to critically read existing work, assess research claims and supporting evidence, identify open problems, and develop an initial proposal for their group project.
        
      
      
        Week 03
        
          Mining Software Repositories and Software Analytics
          This week explores how source code, version histories, issue reports, code reviews, and execution logs can provide insights into software development and support task automation. Topics include data collection, feature and label design, classification, regression, clustering, and deep learning. Students will learn to construct research datasets and examine how data quality, sampling bias, and data leakage affect their findings.
        
      
      
        Week 04
        
          Code Representation Learning and Pretraining
          This week examines code representation learning and language model pretraining, covering tokenization, model architectures, training data, and pretraining objectives. Examples include code completion, masked language modeling, and fill-in-the-middle training. Students will explore how data and training objectives shape model capabilities, and learn to prepare training examples and conduct small-scale training experiments.
          
            Check Reading List:19 papers
            
              code2vec: Learning Distributed Representations of CodeUri Alon, Meital Zilberstein, Omer Levy, et al., POPL, 2019.
              CodeBERT: A Pre-Trained Model for Programming and Natural LanguagesZhangyin Feng, Daya Guo, Duyu Tang, et al., Findings of EMNLP, 2020.
              CodeXGLUE: A Machine Learning Benchmark Dataset for Code Understanding and GenerationShuai Lu, Daya Guo, Shuo Ren, et al., NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks Track, 2021.
              Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on CodeMark Chen, Jerry Tworek, Heewoo Jun, et al., OpenAI Technical Report, 2021.
              Efficient Training of Language Models to Fill in the MiddleMohammad Bavarian, Heewoo Jun, Nikolas Tezak, et al., OpenAI Technical Report, 2022.
              CodeGen: An Open Large Language Model for Code with Multi-Turn Program SynthesisErik Nijkamp, Bo Pang, Hiroaki Hayashi, et al., ICLR, 2023.
              CodeGen2: Lessons for Training LLMs on Programming and Natural LanguagesErik Nijkamp, Hiroaki Hayashi, Caiming Xiong, et al., Salesforce Technical Report, 2023.
              Textbooks Are All You NeedSuriya Gunasekar, Yi Zhang, Jyoti Aneja, et al., Microsoft Research Technical Report, 2023.
              Code Llama: Open Foundation Models for CodeBaptiste Rozière, Jonas Gehring, Fabian Gloeckle, et al., Meta AI Technical Report, 2023.

        Week 13
        
          Research Project Presentations I
          The first set of groups will present their research projects and papers, covering the research questions, related work, methods, experimental results, and limitations. Through demonstrations, questions, and peer feedback, students will explain how the evidence supports their contributions, discuss reproducibility, and identify revisions needed to strengthen their work.
        
      
      
        Week 14
        
          Research Project Presentations II
          The remaining groups will present their research projects and papers, covering the research questions, related work, methods, experimental results, and limitations. Through demonstrations, questions, and peer feedback, students will explain how the evidence supports their contributions, discuss reproducibility, and identify revisions needed to strengthen their work.
        
      
      
        Week 15
        
          Project Revisions and Research Artifacts
          Groups will present their revisions and respond to feedback from earlier sessions. Discussions will focus on additional evidence, changes to methods or conclusions, remaining limitations, and reproducibility. Students will refine their papers and research artifacts, justify their final claims, and identify the work needed before submission to a research venue.
